processing: Leaves of the garden raspberry, Rubus idaeus, are dried and cut with no further processing.
harvest_season: Not tied to a prized picking; sold dried year round.
appearance_dry: Crumbly cut leaf, dull green with paler, slightly downy undersides.
appearance_liquor: Clear greenish gold to light amber as it strengthens.
taste_profile: Nothing like raspberries: a mild cup often compared to a light black tea, with some fruitiness and a tannic grip that grows the longer it steeps.

brewing.notes: About a tablespoon per cup, steeped 5 to 10 minutes. Beyond 10 minutes the tannins turn drying.

vintage_note: Sold with no vintage, loose or in bags, under a best-before date. As with other dried leaf, the fresher pack is better. Packs can be marketed heavily at pregnant women, and that claim is not well supported.
description:
Raspberry leaf tea is made from the leaf of the garden raspberry and tastes nothing like the fruit. If you want raspberry flavour, this is the wrong bag; if you want something close to a soft black tea without caffeine, it is a good one.

The leaf is simply dried and cut, and its tannins set the character, giving the cup real structure for a herbal.

Water just off the boil and 5 to 10 minutes works well, and steeping much longer than that dries the mouth. It is also good cold.

Its fame comes from pregnancy lore: it has long been recommended as an aid to childbirth. Research has found little to no support, and a 2009 review called the recommendations questionable and raised concern over the missing safety evidence. Anyone pregnant should ask a midwife or doctor rather than go by the packet.
history:
Raspberry leaf belongs to folk medicine, and it is listed as a herbal drug under the name Rubi idaei folium. Russian herbal tradition uses raspberry tea as a remedy for sweating out a cold, and English-speaking lore connects the leaf with childbirth.

The evidence for the childbirth use is largely anecdotal, and how far back the custom goes is not reliably dated. A 2009 review pointed out the absence of good evidence on safety or efficacy.
